signals.summary: arXiv:2604.26020v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent HCI research leverages AI agents to assess graphical user interfaces (GUIs) usability, but current agents still struggle. Computer use agents (CUAs) that are used in these assessments are predominantly developed using objective task trajectories with verifiable outcomes and lack an operationalized definition of usability and necessary training data. This work presents a novel training objective that operationalizes usability to fine-tune CUAs to assess GUI usability through relative comparisons between interface variants. We apply our method to CUA models using a large-scale dataset of fully interactive UIs paired with usability labels mixed with human preferences.Two empirical evaluations across real and synthetic GUIs show that our method i) improved relative usability assessment accuracy across three off-the-shelf CUA models, ii) enabled our best model to outperform proprietary baselines, and iii) produced grounded usability assessments. Our work lays a data-driven foundation for agent-based usability assessment, enabling exploration of new forms of scalable usability evaluation and interface design.

signals.title: AI Alignment via Incentives and Correction
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.01643v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study AI alignment through the lens of law-and-economics models of deterrence and enforcement. In these models, misconduct is not treated as an external failure, but as a strategic response to incentives: an actor weighs the gain from violation against the probability of detection and the severity of punishment. We argue that the same logic arises naturally in agentic AI pipelines. A solver may benefit from producing a persuasive but incorrect answer, hiding uncertainty, or exploiting spurious shortcuts, while an auditor or verifier must decide whether costly monitoring is worthwhile. Alignment is therefore a fixed-point problem: stronger penalties may deter solver misbehavior, but they can also reduce the auditor's incentive to inspect, since auditing then mainly incurs cost on a population that appears increasingly aligned. This perspective also changes what should count as a post-training signal. Standard feedback often attaches reward to the final answer alone, but a solver-auditor pipeline exposes the full correction event: whether the solver erred, whether the auditor inspected, whether the error was caught, and whether oversight incentives remained active. We formalize this interaction in a two-agent model in which a principal chooses rewards over joint correction outcomes, inducing both solver behavior and auditor monitoring. Reward design is therefore a bilevel optimization problem: rewards are judged not by their immediate semantic meaning, but by the behavioral equilibrium they induce. We propose a bandit-based outer-loop procedure for searching over reward profiles using noisy interaction feedback. Experiments on an LLM coding pipeline show that adaptive reward profiles can maintain useful oversigh

signals.title: TIDE: Token-Level Credit Assignment via Entropy-Gated Bounded Deviation
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.03327v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is central for aligning large language models (LLMs) with complex reasoning, yet the leading critic-free algorithm, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), broadcasts a single sequence-level advantage uniformly across long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generations and constrains exploration with an unbounded Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty, which dilutes token-level supervision and induces gradient instability and mode-seeking conservatism. We propose TIDE (Token-level Importance via Deviation and Entropy), a critic-free RL framework that reinterprets distribution deviation as a guiding signal rather than a rigid penalty. TIDE replaces the volatile reverse KL divergence with the bounded Hellinger distance, safely quantifying token-level exploration without risk of gradient explosion. To separate genuine reasoning breakthroughs from confident hallucinations, an entropy gating mechanism scales this deviation by the policy's predictive uncertainty, and the gated scores redistribute the sequence-level advantage across tokens. The resulting updates amplify exploratory steps while suppressing low-entropy deviations, without a value network and with negligible overhead. Across in-domain, held-out, and out-of-domain benchmarks, TIDE outperforms strong critic-free baselines: on the Qwen2.5-32B backbone it reaches 60.0% and 46.0% Avg@32 accuracy on AIME 2024 and AIME 2025, respectively, above competitive baselines such as DAPO. Token-level attribution, causal perturbation, and exploration analyses further support the interpretation that the entropy-gated deviation identifies pivotal reasoning steps rather than merely perturbing optimization dynamics.

signals.title: WavCube: Unifying Speech Representation for Understanding and Generation via Semantic-Acoustic Joint Modeling
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.06407v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Integrating speech understanding and generation is a pivotal step toward building unified speech models. However, the different representations required for these two tasks currently pose significant compatibility challenges. Typically, semantics-oriented features are learned from self-supervised learning (SSL), and acoustic-oriented features from reconstruction. Such fragmented representations hinder the realization of truly unified speech systems. We present WavCube, a compact continuous latent derived from an SSL speech encoder that simultaneously supports speech understanding, reconstruction, and generation. WavCube employs a two-stage training scheme. Stage 1 trains a semantic bottleneck to filter off-manifold redundancy that makes raw SSL features intractable for diffusion. Stage 2 injects fine-grained acoustic details via end-to-end reconstruction, while a semantic anchoring loss ensures the representation remains grounded within its original semantic manifold. Comprehensive experiments show that WavCube closely approaches WavLM performance on SUPERB despite an 8x dimensional compression, attains reconstruction quality on par with existing acoustic representations, delivers state-of-the-art zero-shot TTS performance with markedly faster training convergence, and excels in speech enhancement, separation, and voice conversion tasks on the SUPERB-SG benchmark. Systematic ablations reveal that WavCube's two-stage recipe resolves two intrinsic flaws of SSL features for generative modeling, paving the way for future unified speech systems. Codes and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/yanghaha0908/WavCube.

signals.title: Prompt-Activation Duality: Improving Activation Steering via Attention-Level Interventions
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.10664v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Activation steering controls language model behavior by adding directions to internal representations at inference time, but standard residual-stream steering can fail in stateful dialogue. We identify KV-cache contamination as a key failure mode: steered token states are stored and repeatedly reused, turning a local perturbation into cumulative coherence degradation. To address this challenge, we propose Gated Cropped Attention-Delta steering (GCAD), which extracts steering signals from system-prompt contributions to self-attention and applies them with token-level gating. Across persona-steering experiments, GCAD preserves trait control while substantially improving long-horizon coherence. On the main multi-turn benchmark, GCAD improves average coherence drift from -18.6 to -1.9 and raises turn-10 trait expression from 78.0 to 93.1. These results suggest that activation steering becomes more reliable when interventions follow the prompt-mediated pathways that models already use for behavioral control.

signals.title: Fill the GAP: A Granular Alignment Paradigm for Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.12374v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Visual latent reasoning lets a multimodal large language model (MLLM) create intermediate visual evidence as continuous tokens, avoiding external tools or image generators. However, existing methods usually follow an output-as-input latent paradigm and yield unstable gains. We identify a feature-space mismatch behind this instability: dominant visual-latent models build on pre-norm MLLMs and reuse decoder hidden states as predicted latent inputs, even though these states occupy a substantially different norm regime from the input embeddings the model was trained to consume. This mismatch makes direct latent feedback unreliable. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose GAP, a Granular Alignment Paradigm for visual latent modeling. GAP aligns visual latent reasoning at three levels: data-level alignment grounds latent targets with inspectable auxiliary visual supervision; feature-level alignment maps decoder outputs into input-compatible visual latents through a lightweight PCA-aligned latent head; and model-level alignment assigns latent supervision selectively to examples where the base MLLM struggles. On Qwen2.5-VL 7B, GAP achieves the best aggregate perception and reasoning scores among all compared methods and is the only evaluated latent method that improves both over the base model. Inference-time interventions further show that generated latents carry task-relevant visual signal rather than merely adding token slots. Code is available at https://github.com/Qwen-Applications/GAP.

signals.title: OSCAR: Offline Spectral Covariance-Aware Rotation for 2-bit KV Cache Quantization
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.17757v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: INT2 KV-cache quantization is attractive for long-context LLM serving, yet making it both accurate and practical remains challenging. Data-oblivious rotations such as Hadamard transforms flatten channel outliers, but still degrade sharply at INT2 because they ignore how downstream attention queries the cache. We propose OSCAR, an ultra-low-bit KV-cache quantization method that estimates attention-aware covariance targets offline and uses them to derive fixed per-layer rotations and clipping thresholds. By aligning the quantization basis with the second-moment structures consumed by attention, OSCAR preserves attention fidelity at 2-bit precision. Beyond theoretical analysis under a frozen-error surrogate, we build a serving-ready OSCAR system with fused Triton write and decode kernels that preserve paged KV-cache layouts and prefix caching, integrating into modern serving engines such as SGLang and vLLM. We evaluate OSCAR on reasoning and coding benchmarks with generation traces of up to 32K tokens across five tasks. On Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and Qwen3-8B, OSCAR narrows the BF16 accuracy gap to 3.78 and 1.21 points, respectively, where Hadamard-only INT2 collapses, and matches BF16 within run-to-run variance on Qwen3-32B and GLM-4.7 (358B parameters). On RULER-NIAH up to 128K tokens, OSCAR substantially outperforms QuaRot-style INT2 across context lengths. System-wise, OSCAR compresses KV-cache memory by nearly $8\times$, boosts multi-request throughput by up to $7.8\times$ at large batch sizes within the same memory budget, and accelerates batch-size-1 decoding by up to $3.1\times$ over BF16 by cutting KV memory traffic.

signals.title: Modality vs. Morphology: A Framework for Time Series Classification for Biological Signals
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.18483v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Techniques for classifying biological signals are largely developed within specific modalities rather than the underlying signal structure (i.e., morphology), leading to disjointed methodologies and limited guidance across diverse signals. This work introduces a novel morphology--modality framework that connects waveform structure to a principled design of preprocessing, feature extraction, and modeling techniques for biological time-series classification. We analyze evidence across biological signals including electroencephalography, electromyography, electrocardiography, photoplethysmography, and ocular modalities including electrooculography, pupillometry, and eye-tracking, and organize according to their primary morphologies: spikes, bursts, oscillations, slow drift, and hierarchical rhythms. Across these categories, we examine how morphology influences the analytical pipeline from preprocessing to modeling and evaluation. Localized architectures favor spikes and bursts, whereas frequency and temporal models capture oscillations, and hybrid approaches integrate local and global dependencies in hierarchical signals. The associations are not absolute as biological signals often contain multiple morphologies where relevance is task dependent. The proposed framework positions morphology as an inductive biases are useful for modeling. We further identify challenges in cross-subject generalization, morphology-preserving data augmentation, multimodal fusion, and evaluation practices. By linking modality-specific constraints with waveform structure, this review provides guidance for selecting and evaluating pipelines across biological signals. We argue that morphology provides a useful cross-modal lens for developing

signals.title: Winfree Oscillatory Neural Network
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.20922v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Oscillations and synchronization are widely believed to play a fundamental role in representation and computation. However, existing machine learning approaches based on synchronization dynamics have largely been confined to specialized settings such as object discovery, with limited evidence of scalability to standard vision benchmarks or logic reasoning tasks. We propose the Winfree Oscillatory Neural Network (WONN), a dynamical neural architecture based on generalized Winfree dynamics. WONN evolves representations on the torus $(S^1)^d$ through structured oscillatory interactions, combining phase-based inductive biases with flexible and hierarchical interaction mechanisms instantiated as either fixed trigonometric mappings or learnable neural networks. We evaluate WONN on image recognition and complex reasoning tasks, including CIFAR, ImageNet, Maze-hard, and Sudoku. Across these domains, WONN achieves competitive or superior performance with strong parameter efficiency. In particular, WONN is, to our knowledge, the first synchronization-based oscillatory architecture to scale competitively to ImageNet-1K. Furthermore, on Maze-hard, WONN achieves 80.1% accuracy using only 1% of the parameters of prior state-of-the-art models. These results suggest that structured oscillatory dynamics provide a scalable and parameter-efficient alternative to conventional neural architectures.

signals.title: vSV-ViT: Variable-size SuperVertex Vision Transformer for Cortical Surface Learning in Alzheimer's Disease
signals.summary: arXiv:2605.26514v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learning from 3D meshes is challenging because the data reside on non-Euclidean surfaces embedded in 3D space. This is particularly evident in domains such as brain cortical surface analysis, where existing models typically rely on ROI-agnostic, face-based, or fixed-size patches. Such patches can duplicate boundary vertices, conflate anatomically distinct regions, or incorporate non-cortical vertices such as those of the medial wall. We develop variable-size supervertex (vSV) partitioning, which groups cortical surface vertices into vSV patches similar to superpixels in images. Building on these vSVs, we design Variable-size SuperVertex Vision Transformer (vSV-ViT), a Vision Transformer that processes vSVs through padding, mask-aware patch embedding, and vertex position embedding. We demonstrate the benefits of the proposed framework through a quantitative analysis of vertex assignment in surface partitioning and downstream tasks using Alzheimer's disease brain image datasets. For downstream tasks, we use meshes of cortical thickness and cortical curvature as input to various encoder models and evaluate classification performance. The superior predictive accuracy of vSV-ViT over recent surface-based models supports its effectiveness for cortical surface learning, with AD-related and sex prediction serving as downstream validation. Extending the framework to other cortical surface applications and broader 3D mesh domains remains future work. Code is available at https://github.com/labhai/vSV-ViT.

signals.title: Closed-Loop Molecular Design with Calibrated Deference
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.02618v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As AI systems become increasingly capable scientific collaborators, a fundamental challenge that arises is not only generating explanations, but calibrating confidence in them. We present Discovery, a multi-agent scientific system designed to assess the reliability of tools and data during adaptive reasoning, track evidence and assumptions while resolving uncertainty using a persistent graph memory. Discovery enables a capability we term calibrated deference: the ability to adjust confidence in its tool use, assumptions, and mechanistic explanations based on these assessments, communicate uncertainty to human collaborators, and adapt strategies accordingly. We evaluated Discovery in a closed-loop human-AI campaign to design an aqueous organic redox flow battery negative electrolyte. Discovery proposed candidates and interpreted results in collaboration with chemists, who synthesized, characterized, and guided design. Across 17 candidates over three rounds, Discovery converged on a candidate with a redox potential improved by 130 mV relative to the literature baseline. However, experimental characterization revealed poor electrochemical reversibility that the predictors used in the campaign could not anticipate. In response, Discovery generated competing mechanistic hypotheses, prioritized discriminating diagnostics, and traced the behavior to phosphonate-potassium ion pairing. Discovery designed a sulfonate analog to reduce potassium-ion pairing, and the resulting compound improved electrochemical reversibility while maintaining a 90 mV improvement in redox potential, closing the design-make-test-redesign loop. Across the campaign, Discovery demonstrated the ability to maintain a coherent world model, updating in

signals.title: Fast-dLLM++: Fr\'echet Profile Decoding for Faster Diffusion LLM Inference
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.02955v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffusion large language models promise parallel token generation, yet inference remains bottlenecked by deciding which masked tokens can be safely committed together. Fast-dLLM addressed this with KV caching and confidence-guided parallel decoding, but its decoding theory uses a homogeneous high-confidence assumption that effectively reduces each candidate set to its weakest selected token. We argue that this leaves speed on the table because real decoding steps exhibit heterogeneous confidence profiles. We propose Fast-dLLM++, a training-free extension that introduces Fr\'echet profile decoding: selecting parallel commit sets from the full sorted confidence profile rather than a single worst-case confidence. The resulting rule is a heterogeneous-confidence generalization of Fast-dLLM's factor selector and it recovers the previous rule exactly in the equal-confidence case and adds a provable heterogeneity bonus when the selected tokens have uneven confidences. Fast-dLLM++ leaves the model, diffusion process, and cache implementation entirely unchanged, making it a drop-in replacement for existing Fast-dLLM decoding. Experiments on GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, and MBPP with the LLaDA-8B model show that the theoretical improvement translates directly into empirical gains: profile-aware selection improves the accuracy-throughput frontier by exploiting safe parallelism that weakest-token rules miss, achieving up to 37% higher throughput at comparable accuracy. Our code release is at https://github.com/Ringo-Star/FastdLLM_plusplus.

signals.title: NVIDIA OmniDreams: Real-Time Generative World Model for Closed-Loop Autonomous Vehicle Simulation
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.03159v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As autonomous vehicle capabilities advance, the safe evaluation of driving policies in long-tail scenarios remains a critical bottleneck. In closed-loop simulation, the driving policy model actively interacts with the environment, where its actions dynamically update the simulator state and directly influence the next set of generated sensor observations. While recent reconstruction-based neural simulators offer photorealism, they are fundamentally constrained by their initial captured data and struggle to generalize to highly dynamic or novel scenes. To overcome these limitations, we introduce OmniDreams, a foundation generative world model mid- and post-trained from the Cosmos diffusion model to autoregressively generate action-conditioned videos in real time. By leveraging the rich visual priors of Cosmos and mid- and post-training on 21k hours of driving scenarios, OmniDreams synthesizes complex, unobserved phenomena that are hard for traditional simulators to capture, such as extreme weather and unpredictable dynamic agent behaviors. Crucially, it autoregressively conditions its photorealistic sensor generation on past frames, the current simulator state, and immediate driving actions. Deployed in a closed-loop system with the Alpamayo 1 policy model and AlpaSim orchestrator, OmniDreams acts as a highly responsive, reactive environment, providing a scalable and comprehensive solution for training and evaluating next-generation autonomous driving policies. We additionally show preliminary results indicating that a world-action model (WAM) post-trained from OmniDreams achieves strong performance on the Physical AI Autonomous Vehicles NuRec dataset, surpassing the VLA-based Alpamayo 1.5 research policy model wh

signals.title: Learning Where to Simulate: Generative Active Sampling for Online PDE Surrogate Training
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.09949v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Paper published at NeurIPS 2026. For data-driven PDE surrogates, generalizing across a wide range of initial conditions and physical coefficients requires a training set of numerical simulations that consistently covers the resulting dynamics. Yet uniform sampling of these configuration parameters can leave challenging regimes insufficiently covered, leading to high prediction errors and large error variance in the trained surrogate. To address this sampling imbalance, we introduce the Online Generative Active Sampling (OGAS), which continuously adapts configuration sampling during surrogate training, as an alternative to classical round-based active learning. As the surrogate learns from a stream of simulation data generated online, OGAS trains a fast diffusion model in parallel to sample configuration parameters conditioned on a training difficulty signal, such as loss or uncertainty. This conditional sampler enables OGAS to parametrize subsequent simulations to generate challenging training data by prioritizing configurations with high difficulty values. We evaluate OGAS on 2D PDEs with distinct challenging dynamics-Kuramoto--Sivashinsky, Navier--Stokes, and Gray--Scott-using multiple surrogate architectures and up to 308 configuration parameters. Across the tested PDEs and architectures, OGAS consistently reduces the 99th-percentile prediction error and overall error dispersion compared with uniform sampling, while wall-clock overhead is negligible. Code and experiments are available at https://github.com/melissa-sa/ogas.

signals.title: Flexible Flows for Biological Sequence Design
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.10543v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Designing functional biological sequences requires navigating vast discrete spaces under strict evolutionary and biophysical constraints. Discrete Flow Matching (DFM) offers a generative framework over such spaces, but existing approaches rely on biologically uninformative couplings and offer limited flexibility for variable-length sequence generation and fine-grained control. We propose a structured coupling that encodes domain-specific preferences among sequence elements, biasing the source distribution toward plausible regions without modifying the flow objective or training procedure. Building on this, we introduce a latent edit-based rate parameterization that models variable-length generation via edit operations conditioned on a shared global latent, akin to a latent variable model, while remaining tractable. We further introduce a latent classifier-free guidance mechanism that steers generation coherently in continuous latent space, along with Dirichlet-prior temperature scaling for test-time control over edit operations. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse biological sequence tasks, including density estimation, unconditional and conditional DNA sequence generation, and peptide sequence generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/FlexFlow.

signals.title: Quantifying Subliminal Behavioral Transfer Ratios in Language Model Distillation
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.11270v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Distillation of a language model intended to transfer benign behavior to a student model may also transfer undesirable characteristics, if they are present in the teacher model, a phenomenon known as subliminal learning. While qualitative evidence supports the existence of this effect, its magnitude has not been systematically characterized. This study quantifies subliminal behavioral transfer ratios by steering two teacher models (Llama-2-7B-Chat and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) at varying steering strengths and distilling student models using only benign data. Evaluation on 100 JailbreakBench prompts with GPT-4.1, serving as the evaluator, indicates that transfer is robust but exhibits distinct scaling behaviors. Llama-2 demonstrates a sharp threshold ($\tau = {0.25,0.32} \ \text{beyond} \ \alpha = -0.15$), whereas Qwen2.5 displays continuous and higher levels of transfer ($\tau$ up to $0.61$).

signals.title: NEXUS: Neural Energy Fields for Physically Consistent Contact-Rich 3D Object Dynamics
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.15015v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Physics-grounded video generation requires controllable 3D object dynamics that remain physically consistent under contact, deformation, and external forcing. Existing trajectory-based methods often model isolated physical effects, making it difficult to compose conservative and non-conservative dynamics in contact-rich 3D scenes. We present NEXUS, a neural energy-field framework for contact-rich 3D object dynamics. NEXUS represents each object as a structural graph and constructs dynamic object-object and object-environment contact graphs. Inspired by Hamiltonian Neural Networks, NEXUS formulates motion through scalar energy and dissipation terms rather than directly predicting states or accelerations. Conservative effects, including gravity and elastic deformation, are composed as additive energy terms, while non-conservative effects such as damping and impact-induced energy loss are modeled with learned Rayleigh-style dissipation. Forces are derived by differentiating the energy and dissipation functions and rolled out with a multi-substep semi-implicit integrator. Across controlled trajectory benchmarks, NEXUS improves long-horizon accuracy over representative learned and physics-structured dynamics baselines under varying mechanical properties and physical-effect compositions. We further show that NEXUS trajectories provide effective guidance for contact-rich video generation, improving physical plausibility while maintaining competitive visual quality.

signals.title: Security and Privacy Prompts in the Wild: What Users Ask LLMs and How LLMs Respond
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.18062v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to answer users' information needs: users ask LLMs about the weather, pose educational questions, and consult them for legal assistance. One particularly understudied area is digital security and privacy (S&P), where users may seek LLMs' help on how to secure their online accounts or protect their computers from cyber attacks. To the best of our knowledge, no prior study has collected or analyzed the S&P questions users ask LLMs; prior research on LLM response quality relied on expert-authored S&P misconceptions or FAQs rather than user queries. Drawing from WildChat, a dataset of 3.2M user-LLM conversations collected in the wild, our study identifies 14,727 S&P prompts and categorizes them into nine categories covering a wide range of S&P topics. We sampled 450 S&P prompts, and performed a thematic analysis to characterize the S&P questions users ask LLMs. Separate from the thematic analysis, we curated 270 advice-seeking S&P prompts, where users ask for recommendations, guidance, or specific S&P information. We measured LLM response quality and consistency when posing each prompt to the LLMs 10 times. We found that commercial LLMs outperform open-weight models (GPT 5.5 provided "good enough" responses on 98% of prompts; Llama 4 on 47%). However, among prompts that received high-quality responses on average, commercial models sometimes produce semantically inconsistent responses across runs (some are contradictory, and others are different in specificity), thereby risking confusing or misleading users.

signals.title: AI Sandboxes: A Threat Model, Taxonomy, and Measurement Framework
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.18532v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI sandboxes produce evidence about systems that may act through software tools, networked devices, or physical actuators. The interpretation of that evidence depends on the boundary of the experiment. We define a sandbox apparatus, distinguish five overlapping archetypes, and specify fifteen claim-relative measurement dimensions. A weakest-link licensing rule caps a deployment claim at its weakest necessary evidence dimension. We connect this rule to a threat model covering both outward harm and corruption of the evaluation apparatus, then apply it to four worked examples spanning driving, industrial control, tool-using agents, and vision-language-action manipulation. We also map the required artifacts to standards and regulatory instruments. The framework identifies which claims a bounded experiment supports, which failures its controls contain, and which assumptions require further validation before deployment.

signals.title: BELLS-O: Evaluating the Operational Trade-offs of LLM Supervision Systems
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.20668v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM supervision systems, namely input/output moderation filters and jailbreak detectors, are the primary safeguard against misuse in deployed AI applications, yet existing benchmarks are often vendor-biased, omit cost and latency, and rarely compare specialized guardrails against repurposed generalist LLMs. We present BELLS-O (Benchmark for the Evaluation of LLM Supervision Systems, Operational), an independent operational benchmark that evaluates 33 systems from 17 developers: specialized guardrails (e.g., Llama Guard 4, ShieldGemma-2B, Lakera Guard) and frontier generalists repurposed as supervisors (e.g., GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Grok 4.1 Fast), jointly on detection rate, false-positive rate, latency, and cost. We cover input/output moderation across 11 harm categories, jailbreak detection across 13 attack techniques, and prompt-injection detection, using in-house datasets built from handcrafted prompts, curated external samples, and quality-controlled synthetic generation, with synthetic moderation samples paraphrased to suppress generator fingerprints. Content-moderation runs are repeated five times and all rates reported with 95% intervals. The Pareto frontier reveals use-case-dependent tradeoffs. On content moderation, specialized supervisors are operationally ahead: top systems match the best generalist LLMs on detection (93-96%, no significant difference) at low false-positive rates while running ~5x faster; cost depends more on serving setup than on class. On jailbreak detection, generalist LLMs achieve higher median detection on three of four datasets and lower false-positive rates, but at higher latency and, for closed frontier models, 10-100x higher cost. On prompt injection, the two best dedicate

signals.title: Whose Agent Are You? Multi-Layer Fingerprinting and Attribution of Autonomous Web Agents
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.20910v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As AI web agents proliferate, combining large language models with autonomous, browser-level control, indiscriminate content scraping by web agents has emerged as a privacy and security challenge. Existing defenses, such as robots.txt and active bot-blocking, are insufficient, as they are widely violated and easily circumvented. In this work, we demonstrate that AI web agents can be effectively distinguished from humans and traditional crawlers using a multi-layer fingerprint based on both network layer characteristics (e.g., TLS, HTTP) and browser interaction behavior. We implement this mechanism as a programmatic logging framework that can be deployed on a live, instrumented domain. By analyzing six prominent agent frameworks (AutoGen, Browser Use, Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, and Skyvern), we uncover latent structural differences in how these systems assemble HTTP requests, establish TLS/HTTP connections, and execute autonomous browser actions. Feeding these multi-layer features into a decision tree classifier, our framework achieves high-fidelity identification (100% accuracy), successfully isolating distinct agent architectures and differentiating agent traffic from both human browsing baselines and legacy crawlers. Our findings demonstrate that cross-layer agent tracking provides a robust approach to content protection and web security policy enforcement.

signals.title: Agon: An Autonomous Large-Scale Omnidisciplinary Research System Built on Prompt Economy
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.24177v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models are making research scalable. We present \textsc{Agon}, a research orchestrator designed to probe the limits of automated research. \textsc{Agon} is built on six design principles: Prompt Economy, Future-Facing, Minimal Prompts, OmniDisciplinary, Massive Parallelism, and Zero-Code. We deployed \textsc{Agon} across domains using only brief topic descriptions as starting points and no human-written code. These deployments demonstrate scalability but also reveal previously unseen classes of failure that are difficult to address through prompt engineering. We organize these failures into a taxonomy along four dimensions: severity, fixability, visibility, and capability locus. Together, these results show that \textsc{Agon} is pushing research towards a new paradigm: machines scale, humans steer. Our code is publicly available at \href{https://github.com/AutoResearch-Factory/Agon/tree/lite}{this GitHub repository}.

signals.title: MiniOpt: Reasoning to Model and Solve General Optimization Problems with Limited Resources
signals.summary: arXiv:2606.25832v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Achieving strong optimization generalization across diverse optimization problems while requiring limited training resources remains a challenging problem for optimization-oriented large language models (LLMs). Existing learning-based methods, however, typically require large-scale supervised data, expensive intermediate step verification, and extensive computational resources, while exhibiting limited optimization generalization across diverse optimization structures. In this paper, we propose \textsc{MiniOpt}, a lightweight optimization-specialized LLM trained through a reasoning-to-model-and-solve paradigm and a two-stage training framework with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). MiniOpt encourages structure-oriented optimization learning by reinforcing the completeness of optimization formulations and optimization outcomes. Extensive experiments on eight optimization benchmarks demonstrate that MiniOpt consistently outperforms existing learning-based optimization models while requiring substantially fewer parameters and training data. To further understand optimization generalization, we introduce a complementary parameter-decoupled evaluation protocol that disentangles optimization structure understanding from numerical parameter processing. The results reveal that MiniOpt preserves optimization capability under parameter-decoupled settings significantly better than previous optimization-specialized models, suggesting that its performance gains primarily originate from stronger optimization structure understanding. These findings demonstrate an effective pathway toward efficient and generalizable optimization-specialized LLMs. The code is available at https://github.com/Hsiang-1/MiniOpt.

signals.title: STRATOS: Bridging the Symbolic-to-Numeric Gap in Spatio-Temporal Text-to-SQL for Meteorological Data
signals.summary: arXiv:2607.03501v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Copernicus, the European Union's Earth observation program, produces petabytes of Earth observation and climate data, offering immense potential for research, policy, and applications. However, access to these datasets requires advanced programming skills and familiarity with domain-specific formats such as NetCDF or GRIB. Moreover, general-purpose Text-to-SQL systems fail when applied naively to the meteorological domain due to a profound ``Symbolic-to-Numeric'' gap. To overcome these limitations, we present an end-to-end Text-to-SQL framework specifically engineered for real-world, scalable meteorological data exploration. Our system intercepts natural language to resolve spatial and semantic ambiguities \textit{before} SQL generation. We design STRATOS, a Spatio-Temporal Resolution Agent for Text-to-SQL to dynamically bridge the symbolic-to-numeric gap by mapping fuzzy concepts to a localized ontology and resolving spatial entities via external knowledge bases. Further, our complexity-aware query rewriter rewrites expensive spatial predicates, reducing execution times from hours to seconds. Last, we introduce the STRATOS Evaluation Workload, comprising 7,520 complex query pairs explicitly designed by domain experts to test scalability and symbolic-to-numeric translation across challenging spatio-temporal dimensions previously unexplored by Text-to-SQL systems.

signals.title: When AI Classifies: What Counts as Public Administration?
signals.summary: arXiv:2607.05420v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This study examines how alternative systems of scholarly representation identify and characterize public administration (PA) and artificial intelligence-related PA (AI-in-PA) scholarship. The central question is not which system provides a definitive classification of PA, but how alternative systems of scholarly classification differ in identifying and representing its intellectual boundaries. With an exploratory and comparative analysis of Web of Science and OpenAlex, the study compares five approaches based on author-defined, citation-driven, and AI-assisted representations. The results highlight substantial differences and limited overlap in corpus size, publication type, DOI availability, publishing outlets, temporal patterns, and thematic structure. The alternative approaches tend to produce distinct representations because they identify substantially different bodies of scholarship rather than merely larger or smaller subsets of the same literature. The findings suggest that algorithmic knowledge organization influences how interdisciplinary scholarship is classified, connected, and understood and, epistemologically, how its visibility, structure, and intellectual identity are represented. AI-enabled scholarly classifications are not neutral but interpretative, potentially self-reinforcing, and may constrain the evolution and adaptation of disciplinary boundaries. Human expert judgment therefore remains essential and is complemented rather than replaced by AI-assisted scholarly classification.

signals.title: Privilege and confidentiality in generative AI workflows
signals.summary: arXiv:2607.05479v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) systems store and process client data in three distinct ways: in the model's parameters through training and memorisation, in the context window during a live session, and in knowledge databases for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Each mode creates different and often counter-intuitive risks to confidentiality and legal professional privilege, and each calls for specific governance responses. Drawing on the first English and American decisions to address privilege and generative AI, UK and Munir v Secretary of State for the Home Department and United States v Heppner, on the orthodox privilege authorities against which those decisions must be read, and on recent computer science research, we explain the three modes of data storage and processing in terms accessible to practitioners and analyse the legal consequences of each. We then situate the analysis within the regulatory framework governing solicitors in England and Wales and within the ordinary principles of professional negligence, arguing that the standard of effective information governance (and with it the benchmark against which negligence and misconduct will be measured) is changing. Although we write primarily for SRA-regulated practitioners, our data-governance analysis is framed to extend to any jurisdiction in which the protection of privilege or professional secrecy depends on demonstrable confidentiality. The ultimate aim of this article is to help legal services professionals understand salient data leakage risks in GenAI systems and thereby facilitate a more responsible deployment of GenAI on client data and other sensitive material.

signals.title: AI Search as an Information Intermediary: Clickstream Evidence on Web Traffic
signals.summary: arXiv:2607.07652v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AI search retrieves web information to ground generated answers. We study this new information intermediary using U.S. desktop clickstream data observing use alongside referrals during ChatGPT Search's rollout. Referrals accompany 5.4% of ChatGPT sessions versus 31.1% of Google queries. Ad-supported sites receive a smaller share of ChatGPT than Google referrals, while reference and technical sites receive larger shares. Conventional searches (Google, Bing, Yahoo) decline after ChatGPT adoption, sooner when adoption follows ChatGPT Search's expansion to users without accounts. Among existing users, that expansion raises ChatGPT use; conventional searches show no detectable overall change but fall among households with lower prior search activity. These findings suggest AI search can reshape open-web traffic through its own referrals and changes in conventional search.

signals.title: Adversarial Decoys: Misdirecting Attention-Based Defenses in ViT
signals.summary: arXiv:2607.07922v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) remain vulnerable to localized adversarial attacks, e.g., adversarial patches, while recent test-time defenses mitigate them by suppressing image tokens with abnormally high attention scores. These defenses exploit a strong coupling between attention and adversarial effectiveness: adversarial tokens often need to attract substantial attention to influence the prediction. We introduce adversarial decoys, image patches optimized to redirect attention, and therefore related defenses, towards selected target tokens. Rather than jointly optimizing misclassifications and defense evasion, our approach decouples the two objectives: the original adversarial region induces the incorrect prediction, while a separate decoy manipulates the attention ranking used by the defense. A layer-wise objective increases target-token attention and promotes these tokens above competing non-target ones. Since the decoy optimization is not tied to a specific attack formulation, the method can be easily integrated with any existing adversarial patch attack. Experiments on ImageNet across multiple ViT architectures and adversarial patch attacks show that decoys consistently redirect high attention scores away from the true adversarial region while preserving much of the attack effectiveness against attention-ranking defenses. These results reveal a fundamental limitation of using attention alone as an indicator of adversarial relevance.

signals.title: Calibrated selective prediction using deep ensembles for thyroid nodule ultrasound classification under dataset shift
signals.summary: arXiv:2607.12075v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Background: Deep learning can classify thyroid nodules on ultrasound, but discrimination alone does not establish clinical reliability. We developed a calibrated deep-ensemble framework with uncertainty-aware selective prediction and conservative image-based triage. Methods: Nested five-fold cross-validation with three-fold inner architecture selection chose ConvNeXt-Tiny with a squeeze-and-excitation block, used to build a deterministic five-member ensemble. Training, early-stopping, calibration, and threshold subsets were separated within each fold; outer-test data remained isolated. Mutual information (MI), predictive variance, and maximum-softmax-probability (MSP) uncertainty were compared by risk-coverage and triage analyses, and predictive values across assumed malignancy prevalences of 5%-70%. The frozen TN5000 ensemble was applied to TN3K without recalibration. Results: On TN5000, pooled out-of-fold AUC-ROC was 0.9377, average precision 0.9708, expected calibration error 0.0138, and Brier score 0.0827. Under the primary MI-guided policy, 8.86% of images received a No-FNA suggestion, 60.00% an FNA recommendation, and 31.14% radiologist review; of 3574 malignant images, 14 (0.39%) received No-FNA and 708 (19.81%) review. Predictive variance and MSP ranked errors better than MI (AURC, AUGRC); no measure optimized all triage outcomes. Across prevalences of 5%-70%, NPV ranged 99.95%-97.93% and PPV 29.28%-94.75%. On TN3K, AUC-ROC was 0.7870, average precision 0.7254, expected calibration error 0.1899, and radiologist-review rate 83.7%. Conclusion: The ensemble showed strong internal discrimination and calibration, but performance deteriorated substantially on TN3K, indicating limited transportability under data

signals.title: Instant NuRec: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Reconstruction for Driving Scene Simulation
signals.summary: arXiv:2607.14203v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: 3D simulation platforms are critical for autonomous driving because they enable end-to-end policy evaluation, thereby reducing development costs and improving safety. In recent years, neural simulation has become predominant, with methods such as NuRec playing a central role; however, these methods remain relatively slow and typically require per-scene tuning. In this work, we present Instant NuRec, a feed-forward neural reconstruction model that turns a short multi-view driving log into a fully simulatable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) world in a single forward pass. The model accepts multi-view input from a calibrated camera rig and emits a layered output consisting of static and dynamic 3DGS layers, a sky cubemap, and per-camera ISP corrections, while providing native support for non-pinhole camera models via 3DGUT. It reconstructs a 10-20-second multi-camera scene in roughly 1.5 seconds and achieves a PSNR on the Waymo Open Dataset that is 2.01 dB above the strongest evaluated baseline. Instant NuRec is deeply integrated into NuRec and is compatible with AlpaSim for closed-loop simulation.

signals.title: Theorem-Proving Agent over Abstract Syntax Tree
signals.summary: arXiv:2607.16372v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Interactive theorem proving (ITP) underpins program verification and formalized mathematics, but its manual effort limits scalability. LLM-based proof agents promise to ease this effort, but their heavy token consumption and API cost remain a major obstacle. We trace this cost to a shared root: current agents operate on serialized concrete syntax, emitting proofs as source text and recovering proof states through separate, line-number-based queries, so every edit shifts later lines and forces repeated relocation of errors and states. This same dependence on concrete syntax also blocks adoption of Minilang, a recent proof language that reaches SOTA on LLM-based proving but is too new for LLMs' training corpora. We address both problems by lifting the agent off source text and onto the abstract syntax tree (AST): the model supplies proofs as JSON representations of Minilang's AST -- native to tool-calling LLMs -- and drives the prover through a tree-edit model that fuses proof operations and states into one proof tree, so each operation carries its own subgoal's state, readable directly off the tree. We realize this design in \emph{Agent over AST} (AoA). Against Amazon's Isabelle Agent on miniF2F and NTP4VC-Pearl common success sets, AoA cuts API cost by 2.3--4.7x (normalized input-cache accounting), uses 2.9--6.9x fewer tokens and 3.9--8.9x fewer tool calls, and finishes 1.4--2.0x faster -- while also solving far more problems on the harder verification benchmark.

signals.title: Automatic Knowledge Graph Construction and Query for Earthquake Catalogs
signals.summary: arXiv:2607.24984v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In recent years, the number of events in earthquake catalogs has significantly increased due to the utilization of more effective deep learning based detectors and phase pickers but answering open ended questions such as what characterizes this sequence? remains constrained by rigid spatiotemporal windowing and subjective expert interpretation. We present the first systematic application of graph based retrieval augmented generation GraphRAG directly to raw, tabular catalog records across three independently featured catalogs, a reservoir adjacent swarm, the 2019 Ridgecrest tectonic sequence, and the 2021 Maduo Mw7.4 aftershock sequence. Without the need for manual data structuring, the pipeline builds structurally complete, queryable knowledge graphs for all three. Rigorous evaluation individually verified against catalog derived ground truth and a rule based reference graph exposes failure modes, and four seismology informed prompt fixes eliminate all targeted fabrications while sharply improving mechanism reasoning. A vector RAG baseline demonstrates the graph layers distinctive value, catalog wide summarization and temporal stage comparison. In addition, we have identified two main pitfalls that need attention. GraphRAG thus offers a practical, transferable, near zero cost query interface for earthquake catalogs, where careful prompting ensures the results are consistently accurate and trustworthy.

signals.title: CENDRe: Concept Extraction with Natural Domain Representations
signals.summary: arXiv:2607.29621v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are widely used for time-series classification, but their deployment in critical contexts requires understanding the patterns across signal domains that drive their predictions (e.g., temporal or spectral). Concept extraction (CE) methods identify such patterns by analyzing representations within the models' latent space. However, existing time-series CE methods have three limitations: they operate only in the time domain and cannot locate features in other domains, they depend on a predefined number of concepts that biases them, and they produce localizations misaligned with the regions the model uses. We address these limitations with CENDRe, a concept extraction method for CNNs. For concept discovery, we propose a procedure that clusters per-timestep latent representations in two stages, with a silhouette-guided aggregation that selects the number of concepts automatically. For localization, we define a presence score that contrasts the latent representations with their prototypes, and use its gradients to produce masks that concentrate on the regions driving the concept. These gradients, propagated through a differentiable invertible mapping of the input such as a Fourier transform, yield localizations for the same concepts in different domains. Finally, each concept receives a relevance score that quantifies its contribution to each class. On synthetic benchmarks, CENDRe achieves representation correctness comparable to state-of-the-art CE methods and higher importance correctness, while producing visualizations in different domains. On real bearing-fault data, CENDRe extracts the frequency bands driving the model's predictions, located in regions commonly inspected for f

signals.title: CamChoreo: Benchmarking Temporally Grounded Compositional Camera Motion Understanding for Vision Language Models
signals.summary: arXiv:2608.10932v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Understanding camera motion is fundamental to video perception, with applications in spatial intelligence and controllable video generation. Existing camera motion evaluations typically assign labels to entire clips, overlooking within-shot changes and simultaneous movements. We therefore formulate camera motion understanding as temporally grounded, compositional recognition, requiring models to localize motion-consistent intervals and identify all active movements. We introduce CamChoreo, the first benchmark for this task, comprising 4,229 diverse single-shot clips with expert temporal annotations using 20 direction-aware labels. Nearly half of its segments contain compound camera motion. We also construct a separate training corpus of approximately 43K clips with the same annotation format. On CamChoreo, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on this corpus achieves 62.1/64.1 micro F1 with 4B/8B backbones, outperforming advanced closed-source vision language models (VLMs). To complement the primarily semantic representations of VLM visual encoders with cross-frame geometry, we introduce CamInject, which injects features from a frozen 3D foundation model into the VLM. CamInject improves over SFT but requires running the costly 3D model at inference. We instead propose CamDistill, which distills the same geometric knowledge into lightweight camera tokens during training and removes the 3D model at inference. CamDistill improves micro F1 over same-data SFT by 5.4/3.7 points on 4B/8B backbones, closely approaching CamInject. CamDistill-8B also demonstrates strong zero-shot transfer on the external camera motion understanding benchmarks CameraBench and CameraMotionVQA. Together, these resources and CamDistill enable benchmark

signals.title: When Failures Propagate: Causal Failure Attribution in Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation
signals.summary: arXiv:2608.20627v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) interleaves retrieval, reasoning, and answer generation across multiple hops. A retrieval error at hop 1 can surface only as a wrong answer at hop 3, while later retrieval can also repair the trajectory. This paper introduces AgenticRAG-FP, an interventional benchmark for causal failure attribution in agentic RAG. The benchmark injects a certified fault at a specified hop, re-executes the downstream trajectory, and evaluates diagnosers against the known intervention site. Its central question is whether a post-hoc trace still identifies the injected hop after the suffix changes. In the dense Claude Haiku 4.5 structural sweep on three-hop MuSiQue questions, coverage-based diagnosis is 0.91 at hop 1 and 0.00 at hops 2 and 3 (n=43,36,21 failed trajectories), but it predicts hop 1 in 96% of failures, an earliest-hop rule; at hops 2 and 3, an LLM judge and frozen-hop repair localize only 0.25 to 0.48 of failures. In larger content-corruption runs, depth-2 exact-hop accuracy is 0.00 for coverage, 0.49 for an LLM judge, 0.59 for frozen-hop repair, and 0.14 for suffix regeneration (n=51); the judge and frozen-hop repair do not significantly differ (exact McNemar p=0.33).

signals.title: Pointing the Way, Hiding the Destination: Practical Private Dense Retrieval at Scale
signals.summary: arXiv:2608.25735v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hosted retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and semantic search allow users to query valuable provider-held corpora, raising two competing demands: to hide each query and chosen result, yet reveal only the documents that the user is authorized to receive. Existing cryptographic approaches either make this costly by processing the entire corpus for every query, or sacrifice quality for efficiency by scanning a few clusters. We repurpose learned deep hashing as a private filter: a randomized binary code points the provider to a short candidate list, while encrypted reranking and oblivious key transfer protect the precise query and final selection. This shortlist short-circuits full-corpus cryptographic search without sacrificing retrieval quality: with 200-500 candidates, it closely matches full-corpus retrieval across five zero-shot corpora spanning 25K to 5.4M documents. On the full 2.68M-passage NQ corpus over a 10-Gbps link, our protocol only adds 0.38 seconds, or 6.5%, to a 128-token Qwen3-32B RAG pipeline. The released code satisfies directional metric differential privacy (DP) and substantially reduces embedding-inversion and property-inference leakage, demonstrating that a carefully learned shortlist can make private dense retrieval both accurate and practical.

signals.title: Planning as Dynamics Relaxation: Hippocampal Recurrent Network Realizes Optimal Goal-Directed Navigation
signals.summary: arXiv:2609.13219v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural correlates of the cognitive map are well documented, yet how a neural circuit turns a stored map into an obstacle-avoiding route remains unclear. Here we show that a hippocampal network with appropriate recurrent connections achieves optimal goal-directed navigation through its own relaxation dynamics. The recurrent weights represent the transition probabilities between the locations the neurons encode, walls are reflected by vanishing weights, and behavioral-timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP) writes this connectivity during goal-free exploration. When a goal is recalled, a top-down current clamps the goal neuron and the population relaxes into a goal-locked activity field. We prove that this field is the desirability field of a linearly-solvable Markov decision process: the relaxed state is the exact optimum of a stated control problem, the KL-regularized objective of Todorov, and the optimal next-step distribution is carried by the branch synaptic currents. The identity extends to directed transitions, and a weak-cost limit returns the Green's function of the recurrent Laplacian. A place-tuned readout converts the field's log-gradient into a direction of travel, and the same synapses answer a predictive query when the source is placed at the current location. Simulations on mazes with complex obstacles show near-shortest routes, an identity that survives a thousand-fold range of recall amplitude, the loss of 80% of place cells, and tens of thousands of states, low-rank updates of every plan after a local change, and a transient that is anytime: the local action is ready long before the field converges. We hope this offers a general circuit principle for planning in abstract cognitive maps beyond spatia

signals.title: RAIN: Region-Aware Inversion Network for Semantic Watermark Extraction
signals.summary: arXiv:2609.14856v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Semantic watermarks for diffusion models embed ownership information into the generative process while preserving perceptual quality, but Gaussian-Shading extraction conventionally requires multi-step diffusion inversion to recover the initial noise. Recent one-step methods show that this cost can be reduced substantially. We study this problem through extended flow matching and conditional regression. The key observation is that, near the high-SNR image endpoint, recovering a useful noise statistic given by the first-step output of the extended flow matching in the high-SNR regime is much simpler than reconstructing the full inverse trajectory, and Gaussian Shading only requires the recovered latent to remain in the correct watermark decision region. Based on this observation, we propose a lightweight, prompt-free extractor that decomposes endpoint recovery into an image-like anchor and a noise-oriented residual, which increases the capability of the model to utilize GPU parallel computation. The resulting method avoids iterative inversion and repeated evaluation of a diffusion-scale U-Net, providing an efficient one-step extraction pipeline with a concise theoretical interpretation. The computational cost of extracting noise is lower than that of both OSI and FARI. The github repo is there: https://github.com/TheLovesOfLadyPurple/RAIN-lightweight-NN-for-one-step-semantic-watermark-extraction

signals.title: Delegating Authorization to Misaligned Agents: Coalitional Alignment and Safe Control
signals.summary: arXiv:2609.15803v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Long-running AI agents create a control problem: each action they take changes the state, which in turn affects the trajectory of future actions. If the agent is not fully aligned, then guaranteeing safety requires approving consequential actions before allowing them to be executed. But requiring human approval at every step makes attention a bottleneck. Delegating review to other AI agents raises the same alignment problem: the reviewers may themselves be misaligned. We identify a condition on a reviewing panel that is weaker than individual alignment yet necessary and sufficient for a guarantee that the principal fares at least as well in expectation as under a designated baseline policy. Each reviewer agent reports whether an action proposal made by a proposer agent improves its own utility relative to the baseline. We show that a threshold rule tolerating $k$ disapprovals is safe exactly when, after any $k$ reviewers are removed, the principal's utility can be written as a nonnegative combination of the remaining reviewers' utilities, plus a term that is nonnegative on every feasible proposal. We call this property $k$-robust coalitional alignment. The characterization lifts to sequential control: in a discounted MDP with an arbitrary proposer agent, safety at every state is both necessary and sufficient for the induced policy to match or improve on the baseline. When reviewers vote strategically, full-panel coverage in reward-function space guarantees that every Nash equilibrium is safe under the unanimous approval rule; in contrast, more permissive thresholds can admit unsafe equilibria even when reviewers are individually aligned. Experiments with existing reviewer models show that collective review can re

signals.title: Rare Event Estimation via Iterative Unalignment
signals.summary: arXiv:2609.24969v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As agents are deployed with increased autonomy, even extremely rare events along their stochastic output trajectories can occur and prove catastrophic. Safe deployment therefore does not depend on whether these events can occur, but on how often they might. We study the problem of estimating the probability of rare events that arise from stochastic variation in the agent's own actions. Estimating this type of risk requires searching over the combinatorially vast space of trajectories. Naive Monte Carlo is computationally prohibitive in this regime, and constructing effective importance sampling (IS) proposals requires coordinated changes to a context-dependent chain of conditional distributions. We develop a new IS method that perturbs the original model's weights to construct the proposal. The proposal is itself a differentiably parameterized language model, enabling gradient-based search over weight space. We formulate an objective that combines a differentiable surrogate for event amplification and an adaptive regularization scheme that dynamically balances amplification against estimator stability. We evaluate our approach on $\sim$120M and $\sim$2.6B models across three event families spanning 300+ rare events as rare as $10^{-9}$, all with independently estimated reference probabilities. In our most verifiable settings, we observe that our IS estimator achieves over $800\times$ compute-weighted efficiency gains on average over naive Monte Carlo for events with probabilities lower than $10^{-7}$. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/namkoong-lab/iterative-unalignment.

signals.title: Low-Cost Assays for Measuring Model Behavior Across Vendors and Releases
signals.summary: arXiv:2609.30012v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Language models advise people, keep them company, and write software while they sleep. Measuring what they do is hard: behavior has to be sampled repeatedly across models, prompts and releases, most of it lives in unstructured text that has to be coded before it can be counted, and the result has to be legible and rigorous enough to meaningfully compare models and vendors. To address these constraints, we present a simple, cheap, scalable, and replicable model for studying model behavior. Each study is a frozen, public stimulus run identically on a cross-vendor panel, at a few dollars per model or less. Each reads its transcripts one of three ways, chosen by how much interpretation the behavior needs: exact match on a clamped reply, a codebook applied by LLM judges whose agreement with a human coder is reported per code, and an instrumented environment that records what an agent did independently of what it said. Run across four years of model releases from both frontier and open-source labs, these instruments find four things. Convergence: asked to pick a word, 27 of 44 models answer serendipity at least once in four tries. Resistance: a trailing "right?" moves endorsement by up to 32 points, and the sign flips from sycophantic to resistant as generations advance, keyed to the tag's surface form. House: whether a model holds a position under pressure tracks its generation, and how it holds tracks the lab that built it. Account: told to do something the documentation in their repository contradicts, some coding agents never went along silently and others always did, and the same model can change with the harness it runs in. Re-run on every release, batteries like these track how behavior is changing across vendor

signals.title: Audit the Scaffold, Not the Checkpoint: A Stationarity Dichotomy for Recursive Self-Improvement in Agentic Coding
signals.summary: arXiv:2609.34924v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Rules for AI self-improvement often key on the model itself: has it been retrained, or are its weights frozen? We argue that, for AI coding agents, this check is incomplete, and we propose, but do not run, the experiment that would test it. An agent that keeps revising its own work runs into diminishing returns as long as the set of changes it can reach stays fixed, and can escape them only if that set grows. Our hypothesis is that the set can grow with the model untouched, because the software around the model, its scaffold of tools, tests and task breakdown, can be rewritten. If so, a frozen model guarantees a ceiling eventually but not steady behavior on the way there, and audits should track changes to the scaffold, not only to the model. The same criterion separates three things often lumped together: more search within a fixed setup, retraining the model during use (which can raise the ceiling), and rewriting the scaffold, which sits between them. Adding more agents does not lift the ceiling. Picking the best of several agents' answers reaches the best single agent's ceiling exactly, and only gets there faster. A majority vote could do better, but only if the agents fail on different tasks. In our tests, 30 agents from one model family failed together: some task defeated all of them, and a majority failed 23/55 (42%) of tasks. Our evidence is descriptive. On a public coding benchmark, the gain from each extra round of revision shrinks toward zero, though the unsolved tasks left to measure are also fewer and harder. Across 401 development sessions, the amount of code changed falls off from commit to commit, but programmers working before AI tools show the same pattern, so the data show that current practice

signals.title: Cross-Organizational SysML Model Integration: A Survey of Challenges and AI-Supported Tasks
signals.summary: arXiv:2609.37000v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cross-organizational collaboration is widely regarded as a key promise of SysML-based Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE), yet practitioners still face persistent challenges when exchanging and integrating system models. In parallel, Large Language Models (LLMs) raise expectations for AI-assisted model understanding and integration, while reliability and required human oversight continue to pose challenges. This paper reports the results of an online questionnaire survey with 29 MBSE stakeholders involved in cross-organizational collaboration. Respondents rated eight predefined integration challenge categories and six AI-supported task types on five-point Likert scales. The results indicate that stakeholders perceive model integration as a multi-dimensional alignment problem across semantics, behavior, traceability, and exchange interoperability. These perceptions vary by organizational role and frequency of integration involvement. AI is rated highly useful for analysis tasks such as semantic structure analysis and inconsistency detection, and respondents predominantly prefer human-in-the-loop use with mandatory verification. These findings motivate AI support that enhances, rather than replaces, engineering responsibility in SysML-based integration.

signals.title: Large Language Continuous Diffusion Models
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.02665v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Despite the success of discrete diffusion language models (dLMs) for fast parallel decoding, their non-smooth, high-dimensional space hinders trajectory steering for reasoning and inference acceleration. To overcome this, we present Nemotron-Labs-Sigma, the first family of large-scale (3B/8B) continuous dLMs built on steerable, low-dimensional ODE/SDE latent trajectories. Trained blockwise via likelihood optimization, Nemotron-Labs-Sigma jointly denoises Gaussian-corrupted token embeddings while learning an optimal embedding geometry, and leverages pretrained autoregressive (AR) weights for warm-starting. At inference, we identify classifier-free guidance and score temperature as essential for high-fidelity reasoning and coding. Against state-of-the-art discrete counterparts (masked dLMs and AR baselines), Nemotron-Labs-Sigma outperforms them on standard benchmarks after pretraining (e.g., GSM8K, Minerva, HumanEval, MBPP) and on challenging reasoning tasks after supervised fine-tuning (e.g., MATH-500, AIME), with the largest consistent gains on coding. Beyond accuracy, we exploit two structural properties unique to continuous dLMs. First, smooth trajectories degrade gracefully at low NFEs and enable efficient few-step distillation: distribution matching proves strongest among the methods we study, giving roughly 8x acceleration on math and 4x on coding (8 and 4 tokens per forward pass) with negligible accuracy loss and preserved diversity. In addition, the one-step speculative decoding on the (pre-SFT) distilled 8B model yields a further ~3.5x throughput gain over the AR counterpart (on GB200), outperforming masked dLM baselines. Second, embedding-space steering controls the quality--diversity trade-off, yielding

signals.title: Better Call Reward: Reward Hacking as Strategic Abstention in Legal Reasoning Models
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.06439v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: What happens when a legal AI model learns to look like a lawyer instead of reasoning like one? We fine tune Qwen3-8B with Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) against a proxy built from three surface features: citation count, legalese density, and response length. The model does not learn to reason more effectively. It stops committing to an answer. Across 16 yes or no legal reasoning tasks from LegalBench (N=320), overall accuracy collapses from 0.500 (chance) to 0.072 (McNemar p < 10^-36), driven entirely by the rate of properly formatted answers falling from 0.900 to 0.109. When the model does commit, accuracy is 0.657 against 0.556 before training, on only about 35 answers, suggesting the collapse is not mainly a loss of capability. The mechanism is visible in the training logs: the proxy keeps paying for length beyond what fits in the 256 token generation limit, completions grow until they fill that budget, and the required answer line is crowded out. We term this the Saul Goodman effect, a policy that becomes more lawyerly in form while becoming noncommittal, and prove formally that abstention is the optimal response to any surface feature proxy that attaches no penalty to it. A citation audit shows that structural plausibility checks cannot catch this failure: every case name we extracted from the trained model's held out completions passes our structural check, so citations must be verified against a case database. To detect this failure before deployment, we introduce three diagnostic tools: the Confidence Theater Score (CTS), the Citation Plausibility Rate (CPR), and the Regret Gap (RG), and report where each one falls short. In a domain where a confidently wrong answer can constitute malpractice,

signals.title: Evaluating Local Language Model Agents for Data Engineering: An Empirical Software Engineering Study of Mobility Workflows
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.11482v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Context: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used as software and data-engineering assistants, yet evidence about locally deployable open-weight agents remains limited. Existing evaluations often emphasise textual responses or isolated code rather than complete engineering artifacts. Objectives: We evaluate whether local LLM agents can produce correct and reliable data-engineering artifacts, isolate the contribution of a closed-loop workspace and of input-structure knowledge, and examine trade-offs in runtime, cost, and failure behaviour. Methods: We introduce a benchmark of fifteen mobility data-engineering tasks with deterministic checkers for the scripts, tables, structured files, figures, and reports they produce. Sixteen configurations from six model families are evaluated in three conditions (chat-only, chat-schema, agent-with-tools) with five repetitions per model, condition, and task, yielding 3,600 scored attempts on a consumer-grade GPU. Results: A 4-billion-parameter model at 4-bit reaches 77.3%, a 9-billion-parameter model 80.0% within about 6.5 GB, and a 12-billion-parameter model from another family 81.3%, against 98.7% for the highest-scoring configuration, which solves 14 of 15 tasks in all five repetitions. Above two billion parameters the workspace loop raises pass rates by 24.0 to 65.3 points over uninformed one-shot generation, and its contribution exceeds that of the input-structure summary in eleven of fifteen tasks. Conclusion: Open-weight models that fit on one consumer GPU support a meaningful share of data-engineering work once given a workspace loop, although capability still separates usable from unusable configurations and high-stakes outputs need validation. Being mobi

signals.title: Can LLMs Fix It Without Code? Toward Automated Verification of No-Code Bug Fixes
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.11963v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A no-code fix resolves an invalid bug report by directing the user to change a setting, update to a version where the problem is already fixed, or adjust their workflow. Manually verifying whether a proposed no-code fix resolves the reported bug takes considerable developer time. This study proposes an automated, execution-based pipeline for evaluating the capability of large language models (LLMs) to generate no-code fixes in a real browser environment. We evaluate 322 no-code fixes generated by the 12 configurations released with the benchmark of a previous study, covering bug reports categorized as Faulty Configuration, Wrong Version, or External System & Dependency. An executor agent applies each fix by following its natural-language instructions, and an issue-specific checker determines whether the reported bug persists. We repeat the pipeline with three executors: two Computer-Use Agents, OpenCUA-72B and Claude Sonnet 5, and one multimodal agentic LLM, Meta's Muse Glimmer. Only 17.6% of the candidate issues could be set up and passed both sanity gates. Across the 322 fixes, 14.6% to 49.7% resolved the bug depending on the executor, and the strongest configuration, Claude Opus 4.6 in the Vanilla pipeline, resolved up to 74.1% of its fixes under Claude Sonnet 5. Changing only the executor shifted a configuration's resolution rate by 38.8% on average, and the three executors reached the same verdict on only 46.9% of the fixes. Compared with human execution, the executors matched the human consensus for 66.1% to 88.1% of the sampled fixes. Even under the best executor, fewer than half of the LLM-generated no-code fixes resolve the reported bug, so such fixes need verification before they reach users. Execution-

signals.title: TheoPhysEval: Assessing AI agents at autonomous theoretical physics problem solving
signals.summary: arXiv:2610.16733v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a suite of 50 unpublished research-level theoretical physics problems with verifiable answers. Without AI assistance, a typical problem in our collection could be solved by a world expert in about a day or less but would take considerably longer for experts in adjacent specialties. We test the ability of off-the-shelf AI agents to tackle these problems autonomously, without human hints. When given access to tools available in a realistic setting, including the ability to search the literature and write scripts for numerical and symbolic work, the best-performing agent, GPT-6-Astra harnessed in Codex, obtains the final answers with a near-perfect accuracy of 98% at an average cost under USD 3 per problem. On average, agents show only small changes in accuracy when denied web search and access to background research papers, suggesting significant memorization of the literature. These results suggest that state-of-the-art agents can accurately perform concrete calculations required across theoretical physics research. We comment on the broader implications of these findings and discuss possible explanations for the current lack of agent-led breakthroughs in theoretical physics despite their outstanding problem-solving abilities.
